report:
## Conclusion

Yes—cranberry products (juice or standardized extract/proanthocyanidin capsules) can modestly reduce recurrent urinary tract infections/cystitis in women, though effects vary by formulation and dose, and results have historically been inconsistent.

Early individual trials gave mixed results: a widely cited 2011 double-blind RCT found cranberry juice did **not** significantly reduce recurrent UTI risk in college-age women (https://academic.oup.com/cid/article-abstract/52/1/23/406427), while a non-inferiority trial found cranberry capsules less effective than low-dose antibiotics for prevention, though still with some benefit (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1105854). Other RCTs, however, showed benefit—especially with higher-dose standardized proanthocyanidin (PAC) extracts. A double-blind trial of high- vs. low-dose PAC extract found improved efficacy at higher doses (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00345-023-04741-0).

The most authoritative synthesis is the updated 2023 Cochrane systematic review (50 trials, ~8,857 participants), which concluded that cranberry products reduce risk of symptomatic, culture-confirmed UTIs overall, with the clearest benefit in women with recurrent UTIs, in children, and in people undergoing radiotherapy for bladder cancer—an approximately 25–26% relative risk reduction (https://specialistnutritionrehab.co.uk/does-cranberry-juice-and-or-d-mannose-prevent-recurrent-utis/; https://cobfoundation.org/health-information/cranberry-vs-d-mannose-for-uti-prevention/).

A more recent meta-analysis focusing specifically on high-PAC-dose cranberry products in women with recurrent UTI similarly found a significant preventive effect, reinforcing that dose/PAC content matters (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2024.1422121/full).

**Bottom line:** Regular use of adequately dosed cranberry products, particularly standardized high-PAC extracts, offers a modest but real reduction in recurrent cystitis risk in women, though it is less effective than antibiotic prophylaxis and benefits depend on formulation/dose.
